demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
She remembers the weight of the steering wheel, the hydraulic cutters, the way the car metal groaned before it gave. It was a multi-vehicle pileup on the interstate, a gray Tuesday afternoon in November. She was first on scene with her partner, Mike. A man in his fifties, trapped behind the wheel, conscious, talking-his name was David. She worked fast. The space was tight, the door crumpled inward. She positioned the spreader, felt the tool bite into the frame. Then a shift, a pop, and the steering column lurched sideways. David screamed. Something in his chest, she later learned-a fracture from the pressure she had applied. He ended up with a hemothorax, a collapsed lung, a week in the ICU. He survived, but he will never fully recover.

That was fourteen months ago.

Now, at thirty-three, she sits in my office with her hands folded in her lap. She is thin, her paramedic uniform replaced by jeans and a loose sweater that she tugs at the sleeves. She hasn't worked a shift in six weeks. Her PCL-5 score was 64, a number that doesn't surprise her. She says she has stopped reading the news about David, but she still sees his face-the moment before the scream, the way his eyes went wide and his mouth opened. She hears the sound of the metal shifting, the crack that followed. It comes at night, mostly, when she tries to sleep. She wakes up gasping, her hands gripping the sheets as if she is still holding the spreader. Sometimes she wakes up with her heart pounding and her husband, Mark, shaking her shoulder. "You were yelling," he says. She doesn't remember yelling.

During the day, she avoids reminders. She avoids the route that takes her past the highway exit where it happened. She avoids the garage where they store the cutters. She asked to be reassigned to administrative duties, but even the dispatch radio makes her flinch. She stopped responding to texts from Mike, her partner, because every time she sees his name she feels a knot in her stomach. She doesn't want to talk about what happened. She doesn't want to think about it. But she can't stop.

Her husband says she is different. She is irritable, snappish. Last week he asked what she wanted for dinner and she threw a glass against the wall. She apologized later, but she didn't mean it-she felt a cold rage that has no target. She feels empty, often, as if the emotion that used to fill her is gone and only a brittle shell remains. She has trouble concentrating. She tries to read a book, but her eyes skip across the page. She watches TV, but nothing holds her attention. She feels hypervigilant on the rare occasions she leaves the house-scanning for hazards, checking her surroundings as if she is still on a call. The world feels dangerous, waiting for her to make another mistake.

She says she used to be good at her job. She was calm under pressure, quick, decisive. Now she cannot trust herself. The guilt is a physical weight, a stone in her chest that never dissolves. She replays the scene over and over, looking for a different angle, a different tool, a different choice. She finds none. She knows, intellectually, that it was an accident, that trauma care is messy, that David's injuries were severe before she touched him. But the knowledge does not touch the shame.

She is here because Mark told her she had to come. She is not sure if talking will help. She looks at me with tired eyes and says, "I just want to stop seeing his face."
